idiom_name: Django model class + instance save()/delete() and the objects manager
implementation_notes: Django's Model is the pattern in its framework-embedded form: a class subclasses django.db.models.Model, each field declaration becomes a column, an instance is a row, instance.save() inserts or updates and instance.delete() removes it, and the automatically generated manager (Person.objects.filter/get/create) is the finder half. What replaces the classic structure is a metaclass that builds the mapping and the query API from the field declarations, plus migrations that keep the schema in step - so the object carries data, row-local logic and persistence without a mapper. Peewee is the standalone equivalent outside Django, while SQLAlchemy's Session plus explicit mappers is the data-mapper alternative; the sqlite3 module from the standard library is the hand-rolled fallback if you want to write the SQL yourself.
code_sketch:
class Person(models.Model):
    first_name = models.CharField(max_length=30)

p = Person(first_name="Ada")
p.save()                                      # INSERT (UPDATE when pk is set)

p.first_name = "Ada L."
p.save(update_fields=["first_name"])          # narrow UPDATE
Person.objects.filter(first_name="Ada L.").first()
p.delete()
pitfalls: Overriding save() without calling super().save(*args, **kwargs) breaks persistence, and creating a custom save signature without **kwargs breaks migrations and fixtures.
A plain save() writes all fields, so a partially populated instance (form data, a copied object) overwrites columns with defaults; update_fields narrows it.
Managers and querysets are lazy: evaluating them in loops or per object turns association access into N+1 queries, which select_related/prefetch_related exist to prevent.
